utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon, everybody. May we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please. For the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we turn this afternoon to our ongoing witness, may I ask the usher to distribute these two documents to the parties. One copy will be for the registry immediately. The Chamber was grateful to receive yesterday a new list of the estimated length of the case of the Prosecutor. And we came to the conclusion that it seems to be a realistic basis, notwithstanding the possibility that the Chamber comes to the conclusion that the one or other witness may not be necessary. But it seems adequate that we already now tell the OTP that the case of the OTP will not be heard longer than the 20th of September, 2002. You find the envisaged following schedule here, and I don't want to read it out. You have it before you. If there should be the one or other objection by the one or other party, please let us know. Because everything is, without doubt, linked to this first deadline, 20 September, 2002. And I have to express the common wish of the three Judges that we would be more than happy if the parties could come to what kind of agreement whatsoever, enabling the Chamber to come to a final decision earlier than envisaged here on this tableau. As regards the documents before us presented by the OTP, the Chamber has discussed whether or not it would be necessary to prepare additional orders related to three different issues where the Chamber believes that there should be additional evidence provided as it is foreseen under Rule 98. First of all, the question, how the documents are related to another. It would be helpful that for a better understanding of the documents before us, and in order to give the Defence the possibility to prepare the defence, it would facilitate the work to have a kind of expert, granting us and giving us assistance in understanding as to the way in which the documents in question relate to one another, in particular, whether the documents can be linked through referencing within a document of other documents in the group, consistency in or identity of language or terminology used in the original version of the documents, or other features common to some or all of the documents. The second issue was what about any characteristics when signing on behalf of Crisis Staff. The Chamber is noting that the Defence for Dr. Stakic contests, as it is the right, the authenticity of the accused's signatures as they are alleged to appear in the form of S. Milomir in both Latin and Cyrillic script in certain documents included in lists 2, 3, and 4 which have been tendered by the Office of the Prosecutor in this case. We consider that the documents in question form an important part of the evidence before the Chamber, and we consider that the determination as to whether there was a practice in the period from 30th of April through 30th September, 1992, of -- among members of the so-called "Crisis Staffs" to sign official documents with a first or given name or an abbreviation on the family name followed by the first or given name, rather than with the full family name. This may assist the Chamber in assessing the probative value to be accorded to these documents. It would be helpful when the assistance of an expert witness would be provided. And finally, taking into consideration the already mentioned issues, we consider that a determination as to whether there was a consistent pattern of conduct or particular methodology in terms of the way documents of the alleged Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff in the period April 30 through September 30, 1992, were drafted, authorised or signed. This may assist the Chamber in assessing the probative value to be accorded to these documents. And therefore, it would be helpful if the Prosecution could call a witness in this case, an individual whose knowledge of the procedure and place at the alleged Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff in the period from 30 April to 30 September, 1992 in relation to the drafting, authorisation, and signing of alleged Crisis Staff documents. For certain reasons, we have not put this in the form of orders. It only grants the right to be heard to the OTP where the Judges believe there are some flaws; and on the other hand, grant the right for the Defence to react in an appropriate way and that it shouldn't be left until the end of this case. So far as regards these three issues, are there any other points to be discussed today? Please, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I just raise at this stage obviously we may need further time to consider the matter, but some obvious things that occur to us. In relation to the first of Your Honours' requests, namely, that it would be helpful to call an expert, as Your Honour puts it, on how the documents relate to each other, consistency and terminology of language and the like, Your Honour, it seems to me that that requires a linguistics expert of sorts. I'm not at all sure where one get the expert from, or indeed how much the expert could say. Your Honour, the point -- I know we've said it before, but the point about these documents are that they were, I think to the largest extent, seized by way of a search warrant in 1997 from Prijedor buildings, and it seems to us that any likelihood of forgery or insertion of documents given the type of municipality that Prijedor is, that is, still strongly under the control of the Republika Srpska, that forgetting about the question of signatures for the moment, the actual documents themselves speak for themselves. I will add, I may say, we will have to establish whether such an expert exists. Secondly, for him to do the examination will take months. And Your Honour has given us to the end of September, 20th of September, to close the case. So can I just simply raise for the moment that as an aspect that Your Honours may want to consider. Now, Your Honours, in respect of two and three, you've asked for some evidence about the practice of signing on behalf of the Crisis Staff using this particular form of signature. And secondly, as I understand it, and I'm afraid I've lost it for a moment, the pattern of conduct within the Crisis Staff. Your Honour, the only persons who can do that would be either members of the Crisis Staff themselves or persons who were employed in a function by the Crisis Staff. Your Honour, those persons are, of a necessity, hostile to the Prosecution in this case. Your Honour, the Prosecution is enjoined to prosecute and to call witnesses which will, as it were, put the case for the Prosecution. If we are, and how we are to obtain the attendance of such witnesses, I don't know either. But if we are forced to call witnesses who are hostile to our very aims, we're put in an impossible position. We can't cross-examine our own witnesses. And Your Honour, we would have no idea what the witnesses are likely to say. In our view, they are not very likely to be honest witnesses. Therefore, Your Honour, for obvious reasons -- I hear Mr. Ostojic sighing, but that's clearly right, this is a prosecution aimed against the Crisis Staff who we alleged are responsible for the crimes that were committed. It is a course open to Your Honours under Rule 98, to call witnesses yourselves. And if Your Honours feel that those witnesses would be of assistance to Your Honours, then we would invite Your Honours to call those witnesses and enable thereby the Prosecution and the Defence to cross-examine. But to put the onus on us to put forward witnesses for the Prosecution who are not witnesses who have come forward voluntarily and who are witnesses I say clearly would have a bias against the Prosecution, we submit would not be in the interests of justice. So Your Honour, those are the points that I raise straight away for Your Honours' consideration. But obviously, we need a little more time to give it our full consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. At this point in time, I have only to add that on purpose, we left it open --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. At this point in time, I have only to reemphasise that it was on purpose that we left it open to the OTP how to fill possible, and I emphasise, possible gaps in their case. And Rule 98, sentence 1, clearly provides for the possibility, even to order the Prosecutor to act in a certain requested way. But we did not proceed this way. We only indicated what would be of assistance for a better understanding what shall be the case of the Prosecution. And therefore, it may be open for further discussion, and I think it would be appropriate to reconsider this. But first of all, let's hear what the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I add one more thing, and that's this, which I have helpfully been reminded of, Your Honour under the definition in Rule 2 of a suspect, namely, a person concerning whom the Prosecutor possesses reliable information which tends to show that the person may have committed a crime over which the Tribunal has jurisdiction, Your Honour, clearly anyone who was intimately involved with the Crisis Staff, and therefore able to give the sort of evidence that Your Honour wants, more than probably will come under the definition of a suspect. And of course, Your Honours don't have -- I heard the warning Your Honours gave to Mr. Sejmenovic yesterday. Your Honours have the right under the rules to order persons to answer questions. But nonetheless, Your Honours may feel that it puts the person possibly in a situation where they are going to have to give evidence which might incriminate themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only one sentence may be added here as regards the pattern of conduct in Prijedor itself. We have listened carefully to the witnesses telling us the names of numerous persons still in Prijedor, and evidently working in Prijedor under the present government. And I wonder how the Prosecution can come to the conclusion, without having at least tried to do so, to say these persons are already possible suspects. I don't want to mention on purpose names, going through that what we have heard from witnesses, I think it's -- it would be an unfair approach to be very neutral on this, an unfair approach to call these persons mentioned there as living in Prijedor and executing their job in an ordinary way, a priori, as suspects. But I think we have made our observations, and we leave it out -- we leave it for the Prosecution to fulfill their duties under their onus -- under their obligation to establish the case. The burden of proof is still with the Prosecutor and not with the Judges. Any other observations by the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there's a couple observations. First, I have to say for the record that I'm extremely disappointed that the OTP would make categorisations about witnesses that they have not interviewed, don't know anything about, and can only speculate as to what they may testify. If she already knows that these people are not going to be truthful and is already calling in question their veracity, I think it just reflects the complete disregard for both the rules in this Tribunal as well as for the sworn oath that each of these witnesses have taken. Quite frankly, I think the OTP is being very disingenuous to the Court. They are calling people suspects and citing a rule to the Court when in fact they don't practice what they preach. In another case before this Tribunal, namely the Krstic case, they had an identical person, General Sefer Halilovic, whose name was brought up here who they brought into the courtroom, and this is a matter of public record, brought into the courtroom and less than one week after that, indicted the individual. They had interviewed him, they have gotten statements from him. They have gotten an enormous amount of documentation on what this individual says. A week after he testifies in that case, they indict him. They bring him back, and now he's back home based on a provisional release. The OTP merely has to make a decision. Do we want to hear the evidence, or do we just hear evidence that's sided in favour of one side without getting the complete picture. I'm very disappointed in the comments that the OTP has made in this regard. With respect to the Court's provisional or comments that the Court made, we can get that expert, and we hope to provide not just a linguistics expert, but a person to establish the interlinkage of that, if we get beyond the Rule 98 bis rulings. But that we only will know later in the year or next year. I also would like to ask the Court, for example, and just for the record our Exhibit D14 which was provided to us by the OTP on May 28th, 2002, was sent to us which had the signature, purportedly, of an individual who testified several weeks before that, and that was -- I think he was not in private session. It was Dr. Mujadzic. His signature appears there. We're confronted with this document and have to ask another witness about recognition of a signature. We don't know why this document wasn't provided to us before, why it was provided on May 28th, 2002, when in fact all documents relating to credibility of witnesses and all documents that they would have in their possession, especially those that are executed and signed by the individuals testifying, should have been brought to our attention, should have been presented to us. With respect to this pattern, et cetera, the OTP also has interviewed numerous, both Serbian and, respectfully, Muslim and Croatian witnesses who can help with that linkage. They have only provided us under Rule 68 evidence that they believe, meaning their subjective opinion, as to what may or may not -- may constitute evidence which would assist the Defence. In their view, I can't envision any document that they would think would be able to be helpful for the Defence, and if so, just like the example of Dr. Mujadzic's signature on various documents, it's not given to us in a timely fashion and not at all. The burden of proof clearly and undoubtedly rests with the Prosecutor. If this case is going to take two or three months longer from the Prosecutor's point of view, so be it. We are prepared, and Dr. Stakic, without consulting with him, I'm confident is prepared to wait and to see if an expert could come through and to, even through a thread of evidence, support some of these far-based allegations that the Prosecutor has set forth here and made both in their opening and in their fourth amended indictment. With respect to the proposed schedule, Your Honour, we do have a comment on it, if we may, and I'm not sure if the Court would like to hear that. January 7th is the Serbian Orthodox Christmas, and we would like, if at all possible, start on the 9th. And if necessary, even have a shortened time for the Defence, or if we could extend it for those three days. It's very important for a number of reasons, not just for our client, but the attorneys and some of our investigators and people who are assisting us behind the scenes. So we would ask if at all possible that we would have the 7th -- the 6th and 7th off and not be present in the courtroom during that time. That's all I have, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just respond to one aspect of this, because it's the second time it has come up, the complaint that we didn't disclose a document which bore the witness's signature. We did disclose it before cross-examination began, as I've explained, and Mr. Koumjian has explained over and over again. We do the very best we can through the searches and whatever to disclose all documents in a timely fashion. Occasionally, documents slip through the net. But to say that they had no opportunity to cross-examine the witness on that document is not true. It was disclosed before cross-examination began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the parties, are there any other comments to make as regards documents, signatures, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are still waiting to get the original document or the original documents in connection with the report that we showed which we only had the translators' version or notes from the translator. It was from a Senad Kubat who received it from the embassy in Zagreb. I believe it was in --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It has been disclosed in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We wanted to see the original, I think the Court asked for that, with respect to the signatures of that document, if I'm not mistaken. But we did get the 245-plus page document which we're in the process of getting hopefully translated soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I would appreciate if the parties could meet on this issue and try to settle this possible dispute. But then I take it that on the documents on List 2, 3, and 4, there are no other comments to make at this point in time. We are grateful, of course, to receive in part, if I'm correct, please correct me if not, in part, the colour copies of some documents, and I think we'll receive others in the future, that we have all those where it's alleged that Dr. Stakic has signed this document, that we have these documents before us in the form of colour copy. And in addition, we requested to have the opportunity to see the originals of the official gazette 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Karper is already -- we have the originals now of other documents that were requested, and I think also, yes, the Prijedor gazettes, as well. Your Honour, there are still other colour copies to be made of the ones that we got here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: With the now incoming new colour copies, we proceed as we did it with the first ones; we added to the other ones only -- other ones with the same number, exhibit number, but to add -1. I am grateful for the work done by the registry in so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did Your Honours want the official gazettes now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll return it at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I can see no other observations to make. Okay, then the witness may be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We try, at least we try, to finalise your hearing today that started the 12th of June already. May I ask you, in order to achieve this goal, that you today please do us and, in this case, the Defence, a favour and answering as short as possible. We have heard your comments. We have heard your political opinion during all these days. And it would really be of great assistance if you refrain your -- restrict your answers to a clear "yes," "no," or "I don't know." May the Defence please take over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Ostojic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, we discussed at some length some of your thoughts or comments that were attributed to you, and then we tried to establish some comments that were attributed to Dr. Stakic in the same time period, namely, May of 1992 through Exhibit SK45, I believe it was. Now, I'd like you to help me with this: On May 1st, 1992, you testified previously, in essence, that the SDS and the SDA leadership met in Prijedor the day after the takeover. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's quite correct. I think it was the day after the takeover. I don't think it was one day after the takeover. It may have been several days after the takeover. I'm not quite certain, but I suppose that it was several days after the takeover.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Regardless of whether it was the day after or several days after, that first meeting after the takeover, the SDS and the SDA met. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been contacts, but I was not there, so I can't talk about it. I only attended one of the talks, and that's the only talk I can tell you about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then let's focus on that one. You attended the one meeting that you said, or at least I believe you said, the day after the takeover, you met at the SDA offices. You met with other members of the SDA offices. And then you went to the SDS offices and had a discussion with them. Is that correct? Remember when you saw the flag and all that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't meet with the SDS on that day. We met at the SDA offices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time -- maybe I could start it this way. When was the first time that you were in a meeting after the takeover with the SDS representatives, or so-called representatives?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only took part in one meeting, and that meeting was, I think, around mid-May. I can't remember precisely, but I suppose it was around mid-May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe in your testimony on page 35, line 19, during the direct examination, you described the people who were present at that meeting, and you described the people from the SDS, namely, "Simo Miskovic, Dusan Kurnoga, Slobodan Kuruzovic, a woman, another man I did not know well," and then you said subsequently Colonel Arsic and Major Zeljaja came. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that would be on page 36, lines 19 through 21, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind? I don't know whether you have it before you the original page numbers now starting with 4.438. It's not on --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am referring to the notes on a daily basis. I don't have it in the 4.000 page, I know it has been paginated consistent with the testimony that has been given. It's just a general question, it's not for purposes of impeachment or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that sound about accurate?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes, all the people you have listed were in that meeting. There may have been another officer, but I can't be sure about that. Two officers were there for sure -- no, three officers, excuse me, were there for sure. There may have been a fourth one. Whether he had arrived there with the other officers or whether he had been there before, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Stakic was not at that meeting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a meeting of the leadership of the SDS, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a meeting between the SDS and the SDA, and the meeting was convened by Simo Miskovic from the SDS side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in this mid-May 1992 meeting that the SDS had with the SDA, post takeover, the deputy of the Municipal Assembly, Dr. Milomir Stakic, who you, through your testimony, said was an important and critical figure in Prijedor, he wasn't even in attendance at that meeting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS appointed their representatives for that meeting, according to what principle and why certain people were invited and others were not, I have no idea. That was up to the SDS and their presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You seem to indicate in a meeting you had in September in Banja Luka where you say Dr. Stakic was present that he was there, because to you at least it meant that he was someone of importance, correct? That's, in essence, what you said, right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's a totally different context. We're talking about the republic level, the president of the republic, the delegates. The municipal officials. As far as the SDA was concerned, on behalf the SDA, the SDA president was not at that meeting. So we could say, according to the same logic, that the president didn't matter. He did matter, but he just simply did not attend that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you from your statement of -- recently -- June 11th, 2002, you state in paragraph 3 as follows: "In my view, Stakic was not a very communicative man. In the meetings we attended together, he spoke rarely, and for this reason I am unable to comment any further about the man behind the facade." What facade are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure this has been interpreted accurately. But what I'm thinking about is when you asked the question, I spoke about Dr. Stakic as an official at the Municipal Assembly. And as one of the SDS officials. In our communication, we didn't meet very often. He sat at the assembly meetings, and he didn't speak very often. Had he been very active, had he been very prominent, I would have noticed, and I would have said so. Privately, I did not know and do not know anything about Dr. Stakic. What he did at party meetings for the SDS, I have no idea. I know that once or several times he was part of the negotiation team for the distribution of positions, and he met with the SDA. I have no idea how he acted in those meetings. That was just my impression, and of course I cannot judge a person on the basis of how that person behaves in just one meeting. So I can't provide a full answer. What I did provide was merely my impression, a superficial one. Behind that facade, that surface, is there anything that's different? I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say on page 16 of today's transcript on line 7, "had he been very active, had he been very prominent, I would have noticed, and I would have said so," is it fair to state, based on what you just told us under oath that, Dr. Stakic was not active, and he was not prominent during the time period that we're discussing? Or else, sir, you would have noticed it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- let me specify this: He was not active above the average. He did not act as a leader in these Municipal Assembly meetings. That may have been due to his position. He was not the president; he was the vice-president, and sat next to the president. So he was not the one who presided over the meetings. But he did sit in the presidency of the Municipal Assembly. I did not say that he was inactive. To put it more accurately, he was not among the most active speakers from the SDS. Mr. Miskovic, for example, usually spoke for much longer periods than Dr. Stakic. As far as I remember, Dragan Savanovic spoke much more often than Dr. Stakic. And that's what I wanted to say. Had Dr. Stakic spoken out very often, I would have called him "very active," active above the average. But whenever I attended, he was acting just as an average member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me with this: You talked about the activity, and I think it's clear, although I'm sure it's subject to debate. What about his prominence? You said he was not prominent, or had he been prominent, you would have said so. Is it fair to state, based on what you just told us today moments ago under oath, that in fact Dr. Stakic during the time in question was not prominent as you yourself say? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, he was a prominent figure by virtue of the very fact that he was the vice-president of the municipal parliament, and that's what counts. He did sit in the presidency of the municipal parliament. If I'm saying that he was not as prominent as certain other members of the SDS, that's because his speeches were not belligerent, and that's a fact. Some other SDS members did make belligerent or menacing speeches, especially as it relates to the army and the war in Croatia. I can't remember Dr. Stakic doing that kind of thing. But if we wanted to get an average of how often certain people spoke, then Dr. Stakic would average more or less the same as the rest. That's what I noticed. I did not attend all the meetings, but I did attend a number of meetings. And I'm telling you about my experience from those several meetings that I attended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's all we want, is your experiences, sir. So is it fair to state that the times you heard Dr. Stakic speak, those limited number of times, he was indeed not belligerent?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that he ever made threats, and I do clearly remember that some of the SDS speakers did make threats. When I say "threats," that's only conditionally speaking. But he did speak officially, and he put forward the official views and positions of the SDS. And in that, in as far he was no different than the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I can just turn, because you made a comment regarding the SDA president not being at some meetings immediately after the takeover, on July, I think, 14th, 1998, specifically on page 420, line 17 through 21, you testified in part: "I believe that several talks took place, several talks were held between presidents of the two parties, Dr. Mirza Mujadzic, and Simo Miskovic. However, they yielded no result." And correct me if I am wrong, earlier I thought you said that the SDA presidents were not at the meeting, or did not participate at these talks post-takeover. Can you clarify that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, please allow me. I think something has been misinterpreted. I will repeat both the question that was asked and as well as my answer. You said as Dr. Stakic was not present at the meeting with the SDA, and he was a prominent figure on the basis of which he was then not present, that's my free interpretation of your question. What I said is that the president of the SDA was not at that meeting either, and just to follow the same logic of your question, then the president of the SDA was not an important person in the SDA, and he was. And furthermore, I said the president of the SDA did not attend that particular meeting, and you said "several meetings," which is different. So I just want to repeat this: That meeting I attended, the SDA did not attend. Whether he attended or did not attend other meetings, I cannot say. I just wanted to say that if some of the officials did not attend a certain meeting, that didn't necessarily mean that they were no officials or not important. In theory, yes, that would have been possible, but not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Do you, sir, have any information or knowledge, first hand or secondhand, that any of the discussions in those meetings, those that you participated and those that others were present, do you know if the contents of those meetings were ever shared with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, don't you know that Dr. Stakic, as early as February 1992, was a man who was not informed of what was going on in the municipality and did not even know what was going on at the republic, much less municipal level? You know that for a fact. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know that for a fact, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I tender to the Registrar an exhibit, Your Honour, which was showed to the witness but not marked. I think they have it. It's the minutes from an extraordinary assembly on February 14th, 1992, if I may be allowed to inquire on this document. It has a date stamp on it as Exhibit Number S -- and I think it was not ever tendered by the OTP, but I'm not certain of that, Your Honour, so if there's any misunderstanding about that because there's a date stamp on, it we would like that to be changed to our next Defence exhibit, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It hadn't been tendered. Your Honour, what happened is in advance, we put a stamp on it, but it wasn't tendered. But we're happy for the Defence to tender it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The next D number, may I ask for the help of the registry, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These minutes will be Number D19, A and B, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand no objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence under Exhibit Number D19A and B respectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I recognise that this is a rather lengthy document, but if I can just direct your attention to a couple points. First, on the very last page of that document, on the B/C/S version, do you recognise the signature of the individual who signed this 61-page document?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads: "Muhamed Cehajic" handwritten. That's all I can tell you about the signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Do you recognise the signature of Dr. Muhamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure this really is his signature. It may be, and then maybe not. I can't remember his signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the signature page appears, just for the record, on page 61 of the B/C/S document. And it bears an ERN number P, as in Paul, 0053104. Sir, if you look at the first or second page of that document on the B/C/S transcript or the minutes, the version, is it true, sir, that in fact you attended the meeting held on February -- either 14th or 17th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did attend this meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think if you look through the document on the very first page, which is P, Paul, 0053044, it identifies you as being in attendance at that meeting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look through this document at certain times both you and Dr. Stakic spoke. Correct, among other people?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did speak, and I suppose Dr. Stakic did also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you, sir, have an independent recollection of that meeting and the things that you have said in that meeting on February 17th, 1992? And before you answer, Mr. Sejmenovic, for the Court, the English translation seems to indicate it's February 14th, yet the B/C/S transcript says February 17th. So I just want the record to be clear on that, it's the same document that we're referring to. Sir, do you have an independent recollection of that meeting and the things that you have said at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in fragments, parts of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me with this part, before we go through the detail of it. Do you remember at that meeting, sir, informing Dr. Stakic that he was not informed about these by-elections that were supposed to occur in October of 1992 and that you felt that in fact he should check with the republic level of the SDS because he had no knowledge and was persisting in asking what by-elections are the members of this assembly discussing, do you remember that at all? And do you remember telling him that he should in fact check with his representatives because he was pleading and saying he wasn't informed? Do you remember that part of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do think that perhaps we ought to go to the actual parts of this document rather than asking the witness if he remembers it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I totally disagree with my learned friend, because the witness clearly stated that he does have some fragmented recollection of the events as they have occurred, so we have a right before, although the OTP doesn't practice it this way, we have a right, before a document is given for a witness to inquire of their independent recollection, and then only after that has been exhausted, if indeed it has been, do we establish through the record what that recollection was or may have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my complaint is that we have had a summary of what it is Mr. Ostojic thinks was said. I think before the witness deals with the summary that we see the accurate aspect of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will most certainly get to the accurate aspect of it, and I want to know if this witness recalls that at all, initially, and he could share with us what it is that he recalls. And let's see how accurate it will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In principle, the Defence is, of course, right, one has to exhaust first of all the recollection of a witness. But it doesn't help much, we are not interested indeed what is the recollection of the witness, but first of all what can be seen from the document. And therefore, it's preferable, yes, that the witness answer with a clear yes or no, and then please proceed on the basis of the document before us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember having said something like this. But to whom I said it, I cannot remember. I don't know whether it was a response to someone else's statement. I know that one problem was discussed as a major problem, and most of the speakers dealt with that issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to the specific meeting, help me with this in terms of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to the specific meeting and what was said, help me with putting in its proper context in terms of a time line, this is a meeting that occurred February 17th, 1992. Can you tell me if it was before or after the referendum for Bosnia and Herzegovina to secede and ask for its own sovereignty? Maybe I could help to expedite it. Sir, do you remember in your testimony --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, it was that period, around that period. Perhaps slightly before, perhaps a little bit later. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I can help you because I don't think we'll draw an objection from that. The referendum was held on February 28th and March 1st, 1992. Correct can he -- we can't agree on that either?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can agree on that. It is a piece of information that exists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This meeting was before the referendum, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, if the referendum was on the 25th and the meeting was on the 17th, it was before the referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was also before Mr. Alija Izetbegovic declared himself of president on April 6th, 1992, of Bosnia and Herzegovina and declared a state of war. Correct? I'm giving you the date to try to facilitate that it goes a little quicker, so if you think the date's wrong, please I invite you to give us a date you think that declaration was made.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, sir. It's a question you asked me yesterday. And I truly do not know the exact date, and I do not know that Alija Izetbegovic proclaimed himself president. There was a presidency that elected the president amongst the members of the presidency, and no one proclaimed himself president. And I'm not aware of that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to get back to this document. Just on that response, had someone declared himself president in an institution which obviously had this organ called the presidency, that would have been a violation of the constitution both in the former Yugoslavia on the federal level, and sir, it would have been a violation of the constitution, and all the laws and statutes on a republic level. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I know the following about that: There was the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there was the president of the presidency. And that is all I know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to this document, specifically page 21 of the English text. The B/C/S text, 32. And I'd like to you share with us, sir, if you think after reading the section which starts with "Milomir Stakic," followed by your name, Mevludin Sejmenovic, if in that context, sir, you felt that Dr. Stakic was informed about "some elections in October," meaning October of 1992. And I'm not sure if the Court wouldn't mind if he reads, because they are not that long, both Dr. Stakic's comments that are attributed to him and those attributed to Mr. Sejmenovic for purposes of a complete translation and accuracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If the witness would be so kind, these two short paragraphs, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Milomir Stakic: I apologise, Mr. Sejmenovic, some elections are being mentioned for October on a number of occasions. I wish you to substantiate this with arguments, who agreed on this, with whom, and where? And then "Mevludin Sejmenovic, about the elections. And Mr. Mutic as a professional journalist, from that standpoint, and as a deputy, please do not speak to me in that manner. One thing. Another thing, I understand you fully because it is an unpleasant feeling when some fundamental and very important things are being said to the face of people, and Mr. Karadzic agreed to extraordinary elections, as well as Mr. Izetbegovic, the gentleman from the HDZ, and even before the elections and confirm that when they met on the basis of the opposition's proposal ten days ago. So please call your headquarters and reassure yourself."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having read that, do you think, sir, that Dr. Stakic was informed of these - as it's been referred to in the minutes here - these by-elections to be held in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the SDS functioned normally as a party, it would have had to be informed. And Mr. Miskovic and the deputies of the SDS should also have had this information, those who travelled with me to Sarajevo. What the internal relations in the party were, that's a different matter, and I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to state, sir, based on that, since you and Dr. Stakic had a conversation at that meeting, at that time, that in fact it's unequivocal that Dr. Stakic was not informed of any by-elections that may have occurred or were scheduled to occur in October of 1992? Is there any doubt about that, sir, in your mind, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, at that meeting, I was suspicious of all the members of the SDS and the deputies of the SDS. And in regard to many of those things they said, I had suspicions as to whether they really thought what they were saying. I believe that their objectives were quite different. So on the basis of what they said, I cannot really judge what they really knew or what they didn't know. But in a party, if relations become more complicated, it is quite possible that some are less informed or some are more informed. If this applies to Dr. Stakic, I do not know. This all depends on the relations within the party. But in the way a party usually functions, he should have been informed of this. Whether he was or not, whether he was told or not told, this is a matter of the SDS, and I really cannot say much about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, did you ever in February, specifically February 17th, 1992, make a statement that said that the SDS assemblymen were fair and correct in their discussion?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I assume that sometimes you observed the work of a parliament where different parties state their positions, you know what the technology of the work is, the technology of work within a party is, and I suppose that you know what I'm talking about. There are delegates, deputy clubs and groups. They get together, they decide on what to say at the parliamentary session. This is also true of the other parties. And on the basis of the agenda, one tries to implement what has been agreed on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your testimony you said it, but you didn't mean it, but you didn't say it, or you don't recall if you said it or you didn't? Just tell me which one it is, or any other option you may think of.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I said this on some occasions. I don't know on what occasions, but I was very open in my work in the parliament. I did everything openly. I think I said that openly. If I said it at that particular meeting or not, I don't know. I spoke of this in personal talks with Mr. Timarac, and Mr. Srdic, the deputies, when I went to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to the B/C/S version, page 59, towards the end of this exhibit, and pages 37 and 38 in the English text, towards the end of this assembly, again, sir, you speak, among others.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found that part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you, sir, agree that, in fact, on that date, you made that comment, that the SDS assemblymen were fair and correct in their discussion?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps for some of the discussions, I could have said that. I may have said that. This was my practice also in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Regardless of who was speaking, from what party, I always stated that clearly. I was never a slave of party discipline. There were such occasions when I said that, but I also said something when positions were not sincere, when policies were being explained but the person speaking had something quite different in mind. Regionalisation was spoken there. It was presented as an economic matter, but it was not sincere. It was not a question of economic organisation but of ethnic division. So it was an insincere policy, and I said this at the parliament in Sarajevo, and I spoke on a number of occasions in that session. But sometimes when someone was speaking from the SDS, I supported him. This also happened. I was not burdened by anything. I followed the course of justice and sincerity in the way people presented their views. When and on what sessions did I tell someone that he was sincere or insincere, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just mention something, I heard Mr. Ostojic say "men" and that's how it has come up on the screen, but is it agreed that what actually appears in the translation on page 38 is a singular assemblyman, so one particular assemblyman, as opposed to men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think if the witness can just read what has been attributed to him, I think it would help clarify the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, can you read that section where you discuss the fair and correctness in the discussions. Just slowly so we get the proper translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And again, for the record, this is something that is translated by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's page 59. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sejmenovic, Mevludin, deputy to the Assembly of BH. It is my suggestion to bring the session to an end. In addition to what I said earlier, I wish to say that we should avoid finding all kinds of pretexts, pretext and ways of blocking this assembly. I see it like this: We have a house, the door to it is locked. And now we want to pull down the house because we cannot enter it. We have the key in our hand now. All we have to do is insert it into the lock, enter the house, and work normally. I repeat, the assembly is unblocked. As you can see from the SDS assemblyman's fair and correct discussion, there is no other possible conclusion than that the division issue is in its final stage. We have a proposal --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. Is it singular or plural in B/C/S, assemblyman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible. Well, there were two or three discussions that were extremely good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm asking, what was the word you used, singular or plural?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe in this case that it is a question of the plural. I think, in this specific sentence, which I have just read out, I think that the plural is referred to, and there were two or three presentations by members of the SDS and supported the initiatives of the SDS. And I believe that this applies to those members, those deputies. And that is why I used the plural. Do you wish me to continue to read this part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't need it either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic. Do you recall, sir, at this meeting, that Dr. Stakic, for lack of a better term, criticised a fellow SDS member, as having fallen asleep during a meeting. Do you recall that ever occurring?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but it is possible, if I look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to page 15 of the English text, and I'll get you the B/C/S text in one moment, and just so we have it in context, can you tell me who, if you know, Mr. Vinko Kos is? Do you know if he is an SDA or SDS assemblyman?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Vinko Kos was a deputy of the SDS. I'm not sure, but I think he was a deputy of the SDS. He may have been from the opposition. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would you be kind enough to look through the B/C/S -- the first ten pages and see if Dr. Vinko Kos is identified and what his position may have been at that time.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found that particular part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me who --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Vinko Kos, deputy of the SDS."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention to the B/C/S version, page 23, the comments that are attributed to Dr. Stakic, and the English text, page 15. And right under, on the fourth line approximately, it seems to indicate that Dr. Milomir Stakic was wishing to apply to Kos first, and then he told him "he must have been asleep, when we SDS representatives gave a report." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall actually Dr. Stakic being critical of fellow SDS members, at this meeting, at the very least?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I see it from the text, he is criticising Mr. Kos because at the SDS meeting he was asleep and wasn't listening to what Stakic was saying then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, at the very least at that meeting, was not in line with the SDS leadership; he wasn't informed of the by-elections to be held in October of 1992. He was, in fact, even criticising other SDS members at that meeting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's not necessary to make any commentaries, and then ask the witness whether it's correct or not. I think we have already an impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I can move to another point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, during this meeting do you remember discussing with the participants of this extraordinary session of the Municipal Assembly on 17th of February, 1992, that there were, in fact, 7 to 10.000 Serbian refugees in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was talk of the refugees, but what the context was and what the number was, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you sit here, sir, today, do you recall that there were in fact anywhere from 7 to 10.000 Serbian refugees who came from Croatia, who were now in the territory or area known as the Prijedor Municipality, or do you dispute that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were refugees, but I don't know what the number was, in the Prijedor Municipality at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair, sir, if a member of your party in this document were to identify that it was 7 to 10.000 or so refugees, would that be something that we could accept as being true, or do you think it was less?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that I don't know how many refugees there were. Someone who dealt with the issue probably knows better. I either know or don't know about the number of refugees. I didn't know. I was not in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as the sole representative of the Prijedor Municipality, the only elected official, didn't you have an obligation to report on the republic level to the republic assembly as to how many refugees were impacting, and the impact of those refugees in the municipality in which you were elected? Didn't that matter to you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, at the republic parliament, we did discuss the issue. But it is a fact that none of the SDS officials, I'm speaking about the officials, did not give me any information to me or any instructions for me to then inform the parliament of that. On some occasions, I had talks with lower members of the SDS, the ordinary members or the members of the municipal board, and I was asked to bring up certain questions. But formally, to me as a deputy, no one instructed me or asked me from the SDS as regards a problem of the refugees. It was a general problem; it was not only common to Prijedor. It was also a problem in other municipalities. I know that this matter was discussed at the republican parliament, that money should be set aside for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were elected as a representative for all the people of the municipality, not just people who were representative of the SDA party. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Did you, sir, inquire as to the number of refugees and any housing questions that they may have and any living questions or issues that may come up with these 7 to 10.000 refugees?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, yes, I did inquire about all the important issues of the municipality. The number of refugees, well, their number in that period grew. First there were 50, 100, 200, then 1.000. And this tended to change. I did not get reports at every moment of the number of arriving refugees. I wouldn't reject such a report from whatever side it came. But I did speak about this issue to the republic bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just briefly before we break, if I can direct your attention to page 10 of the B/C/S transcript or minutes of this meeting and page 7 of the English version of this exhibit, a Mehmed Mesic, an SDA assemblyman is speaking at this meeting, and just for the purposes of establishing how many refugees there may have been, it states down in the second part, specifically for you on page 10, line 5, that "he's discussing approximately 10.000 people who have returned home from Croatia and Slovenia." Do you see that, sir? In fact, he states, I'll quote it the record: "The data that I have may be old, but it appears that the population of our municipality has increased by some 10.000 people who have returned home from Croatia and Slovenia where they were sacked for various reasons."

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then if we turn several pages, on page 25, the English text, I think there's a gentleman that's identified as Dr. Mirza Mujadzic on page 24 of that text, he also discusses refugees. And I think he states -- I'll wait for you to get to it. On page 38, I believe, sir, of the B/C/S exhibit. And in the first or so portion of his statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the first or so portion of his comments that are attributed to him, doesn't not, the leader of the SDA at that time, Dr. Mirza Mujadzic, also acknowledge that there were "almost 7.000 refugees in our city"? And we're referring to the timeframe of February, 1992, sir. It's on page 39, the very first line.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it. I found that part. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says that there are 7.000 or so refugees. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any reason, sir, that you know of, as you sit here now having been present at that meeting, that we should doubt any of those members, that both members of your party, the SDA, are quoted as being given?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two figures are different, and then we distinguish between two types of refugees, after the war in Slovenia, and especially the war of Croatia. Most of Croatia had been destroyed. Many of the factories were not working, and many people who were employed in the Croatian and Slovene companies from Prijedor, they lost their jobs, and they were returned to their homes. And this is a very large number of people who were jobless and who were in that situation. There was also a number of refugees from parts of Croatia where the war was being waged. But the exact number, Mesic here spoke of people who remained jobless for a number of reasons. He -- Mujadzic speaks of 7.000 refugees. I don't know what he referred to, but I think it must have been people from Croatia who were fleeing the war and who were fleeing to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, I remember that the SDA, in fact, spoke of the issue, and the SDS didn't want to have the issue put on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate to have a break now. The trial stands adjourned until 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please continue immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, can you tell us as the sole representative of the Prijedor Municipality at the republic level, what is it that you, sir, did to assist in finding any housing for the seven or so thousand refugees that came from either Croatia or Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we spoke about it in the republican parliament, but I can't remember any details now. What we said exactly and when. This was a problem related not only to our municipality, but to a number of different municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the people in your municipality, do you know where they were living at the time of February 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some were put up in Prijedor, in the surroundings of Prijedor. But I don't know anything more specific about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: We know as your testimony revealed yesterday, do you know, sir, if there was any refugee camp which housed any of these refugees in February of 1992 or in that timeframe generally?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any refugee camps. The Red Cross arranged for the accommodation of some of them. Prijedor, the villages around Prijedor, the municipal territory, Petrov Gaj, Omarska, part of them were in Trnopolje. Other parts of Prijedor Municipality, too. Some were put up with families. Some in school buildings. But I don't really know anything very specific about the Red Cross activities because that was not part of what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain to me, sir, if you can, this by-election issue that was supposed to occur in October 1992, according to the minutes on the exhibit that we've just reviewed, why didn't it -- first, did it happen in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: October 1992, no, there were no elections in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, in fact, from February 17th, 1992, when you stated that, in fact, to Dr. Stakic there was these by-elections that were going to be held in October, in fact, what transpired was a referendum occurred, and there was a separation and a secession of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia also in April of 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the secession of the Republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is that the -- known as Republika Srpska? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said the secession of the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that that happened simultaneously with the secession of Mr. Izetbegovic from -- asking for sovereignty and secession from the former Yugoslavia? Are you telling us that happened at the same timeframe, sir, April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when this happened. But I know that it did happen sometime in March, I think, of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise, sir, at that time, the Republika Srpska, as did the international community, both during the Lisbon negotiations, the London negotiations, and the Dayton accords? Did you yourself, sir, recognise Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina was not recognised by the international community or anyone else, I only recognised my own state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And negotiations were underway on further solutions to that crisis. So there was no formal recognition of any other entity at that precise moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, at these meetings that occurred in Lisbon and in London and in Dayton, were Serb representatives there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know any details of these meetings, as I've said before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the secession of Herceg-Bosna occur, do you know, which is within Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time when you were member of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. While I was in the Bosnia and Herzegovina parliament, the secession of Herceg-Bosna did not occur. That was later on at some point, but I can't remember precisely when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's been some discussion on the formation of an entity called the ARK. Are you familiar with that, the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not an entity. It was a Serbian ethnic region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know, sir, having been a member of the parliament whether or not the formation of ARK was based on amendment 42 of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me why you think it's not true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, because we had several discussions in the Bosnia and Herzegovina parliament, because the foremost legal experts from the ministry of justice put forward legal interpretations of this issue. There was a provision for regions or associations of municipalities to be set up, but not along the ethnic lines and not along the lines put forth by the SDS. So the view of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the presidency was that this was extra constitutional, this sort of region founded in Herzegovina and in Banja Luka was outside the constitution. And that was the official position of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As the SDS -- how the SDS interpreted this later on is a different issue altogether, and I can't enter any legal discussion of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we have the Court's permission, have the witness be handed by the usher Exhibit 131, both A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it's S131, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, that's a document that we previously reviewed which, in essence, among other posts it identifies you as being elected to the Chamber of Municipalities from the Prijedor Municipality. But my question is on another issue, not that. Was there an election wherein Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and Fikret Abdic ran also during November of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell this Court, since you've told us in the past, that the SDA is one that thrives on democratic principles, who of the two candidates, Alija Izetbegovic or Mr. Fikret Abdic, who got more of the votes in this democratic election?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Fikret Abdic got more votes. How many more exactly, I can't remember. But I know that Avdic and Izetbegovic had negotiations as to who would take up the position of the president of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how is it, sir, that the president of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina doesn't go automatically to the person who got the most votes?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the constitution, the position went automatically to the representative of that ethnic group which garnered the greatest percentage of votes in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the first mandate, as far as I can remember. That was the only limitation. As the SDA list only had two candidates, how they dealt with it internally, what the party arrangement was as concerns that, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, help us with this, then: The presidency, not the president of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it consist of seven members?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presidency consisted of two members - as far as I remember, so don't quite take my word for it - but as far as I can remember, it had two members of - two Muslim members, Bosniak members, two Serb members, two Croatian members, and one member from the "other" ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that member of the other ethnic groups called the Yugoslav member, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, in these elections, yes, the member was a Yugoslav by nationality because each party, when they nominated their candidates to the presidency had the right to place two candidates with different national backgrounds on their list, as well as a candidate from the other ethnic groups. As far as I can remember, Ganic, as a Yugoslav garnered the most votes. He was the one who finally took up the position in the presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was Mr. Ejup Ganic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. As I've said before, Ejup Ganic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me with this, as a member of the presidency, do you know whether Mr. Ejup Ganic was a member of which party?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the elections, he was not a member of the SDA. It was only later, as far as I can remember, that he joined the SDA, and he was one of the party officials. But prior to the elections we are talking about, he had not been a member of the party. I think he was a member who came from outside the party and was thus nominated and placed on one of the party lists. I can't remember anything more specific, only as much as I've said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was that an organ which mandated a rotating group of elected officials so that certain nominees would serve for a limited amount of time? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the then existing laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I'm not sure how that was regulated. But this should not be difficult to check.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We're checking on that. But let me ask you this: Did you think when Alija Izetbegovic was selected as the president of the presidency, that he was being selected for a term of life or for a term of one year, or for any term in between that? What did you as a member of parliament, as an elected official, what did you, sir, think?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not up to me to think anything about it. There was a mandate according to which the presidency was elected. Members of the presidency chose the president. And I think that the term of office of the president of the presidency in some periods, I think, it was regulated in such a way as to have a rotation, but I don't know. As far as the question is concerned, there's nothing for me to think it was a matter of procedure and of the existing laws. They had their terms of office, and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, within the period of expiration, isn't it true that on April 6th of 1992, the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed a state of war, and in fact appointed Alija Izetbegovic as president and Supreme Commander of Bosnia-Herzegovina, all the way through to the end of the war, past 1995?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that the state of war was declared. How the function in the presidency was changed, who took over -- what competencies exactly the presidency took over, I know nothing about this, nor do I know exactly when this happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not familiar with the date April 6th, 1992, and you're not familiar with the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic was appointed and announced as being the Supreme Commander of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the fact that he was nominated, but I must repeat: I don't remember exactly when this occurred. If you'd asked me before you mentioned the date, I would have said "no, I can't remember." Too many dates. I can't keep track of them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Now, he was the Supreme Commander of what? The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, later, when the army was set up, the presidency or the president of the presidency, the presidency actually was the Supreme Commander, and not any one of its single members and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, the army had a collective commander, and not just a single person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With this declaration of war that was made by Mr. Izetbegovic, do you know, sir, if any of the civilian authorities continued to function or ceased functioning and became what we've discussed here as either war presidencies or crisis staffs, on or after April 6th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Sarajevo was blocked, it was impossible for the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina to continue to function. And according to the then existing laws, the presidency took over the powers of the parliament, with the obligation to take temporary decisions until such time as the parliament could again meet to accept or change those decisions. And I know that for a certain period, it was not possible for the parliament to convene. And I know later on, the parliament began to meet again. But that, as far as I can remember, was late in 1993, that parliament sessions began to take place again and the government resumed all its functions according to the existing laws.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was Sarajevo blocked, as you've identified? When?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work of the parliament was thwarted. I think it was in early April. I'm not sure about the day, but when barricades were set up around Sarajevo, and the shelling began. It was no longer possible to get to Sarajevo, and new circumstances were created.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who ran the day-to-day activities if the civilian authorities ceased functioning, sir? Who ran those activities? Was it the war presidency or the war Crisis Staff, as established by Mr. Izetbegovic in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know the details about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, having previously told us that you are familiar with some aspects of the constitution, do you know if there was a constitutional provision which authorised that a person within the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina had the right to declare a state of war and to name himself as Supreme Commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you know of any constitutional provision to support that basis?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
