utterances.text: I don't know about any such constitutional provisions, nor am I familiar with anyone having proclaimed themselves the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that I am clear, you don't have any recollection of Alija Izetbegovic proclaiming himself as Supreme Commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1992 April? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I know, which means as far as I can recall, the presidency proclaimed itself the Supreme Commander at the moment when the situation became extraordinary, not the president himself. That's what I remember. And I can't say anything more about this, because after all I was no longer in Sarajevo at that time. So I have only memorized the information that I got from the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a member of the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, do you know who the Mr. Djure [sic] Pelivan was in 1992? Jure.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jure Pelivan was the governor of the national bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly even as early as 1991, until what time I don't know. I can't say with any degree of precision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me during the time period where you were a member of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you tell me what position Mr. Alija Delimustafic held?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, if you as an assemblyman in 1991 and 1992, whether you had any powers or authority to control, supervise, instruct, or in any fashion direct Mr. Delimustafic, the minister of interior, on any of his duties?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As concerns the parliament, there was, pursuant to the laws, a committee within the parliament whose job was to control the work of the ministry of the interior. So a couple of members of parliament were elected as members of this committee, which then drafted reports, asked questions about the work of the ministry. But no, I was not a member of this committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were part of the legislative assembly, correct? The minister of the interior would fall under which part, the executive or legislative assembly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to interrupt. The Bench has shown until now extreme tolerance in both directions, towards both parties, but I think we can't identify any longer any relevance for the case before us. And this question is not admitted. It's an academic question, and it would enlighten us and it would help us for our understanding in the future for the line of questions you're prepared to put if you can give us some hint on the relevance of your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour. Two points on that: One, I think it goes to the heart of some of the issues that the OTP has raised persistently both in the fourth amended indictment as well as through various witnesses. But more particularly I think, if allowed, that the witness will help us understand that during the selection process of the certain posts within Prijedor Municipality, they had to have been approved by the minister of interior. And in fact, that the members of the assembly were not the ones who were subordinate or superior to members of certain functions, that in fact it was the minister of interior who was located in Sarajevo. But I first had to establish if the witness actually understood the position, and understood the gentleman who was in charge there. But I can move on. I have a lot of areas to cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, are you familiar with a discussion that was held in 1992 by members of the SDS to form a council of national equality or the Chamber of Nations?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if in June 10th, 1991, in Sarajevo, there was a meeting for the National Defence Council to be formed, and it was held at the former police station in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting to set up the National Defence Council. I can't remember any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly, if I can just have some leeway to see if I can refresh the witness's recollection, do you know of an Avdo Habib who was an assistant to the minister of the MUP in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Avdo Habib was the assistant minister and then later on went on to become the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Hasan Cengic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was a member, an official of the SDA. I think he, too, at a later stage was the minister, but I'm not exactly sure a minister in which field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't he the general secretary of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while, yes, he was the secretary with the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Rusmir Mahmut Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a professor, professor Rusmir Mahmut Cehajic, yes, I know the person. I know that he was a member of the SDA, but he did not hold a particularly prominent position. And I think he was a minister in the first government of Bosnia and Herzegovina after the first free elections, or an assistant minister. I can't be sure now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was actually vice-president. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know a Munir Jekic [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Jahic? Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Munir Jahic, I know there was a person who had the last name Jahic, but whether that's person's first name was Munir or not, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that since these were, or at least some of these were members of the SDA and that in fact they formed an organisation of the National Defence Council in June of 1991 in Sarajevo, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this. The National Defence Council is in Sarajevo, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me switch the topic for a little bit. At any time as a member of parliament, sir, did you receive or obtain any information that was classified as being strictly confidential or state secrets?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I know that a lot of information arrived in the parliament, and that this information was discussed. Whether some of the information was confidential, I can't remember. As far as the committees are concerned, perhaps I'd better tell you, for you to be able to better understand my position. I was in the parliamentary committee for physical planning and residential planning, residential activity. That was my committee. And problems concerning what I've mentioned were tabled before my committee. As far as other issues were concerned, there were other committees, and those are the committees or the committees which reviewed those other issues. As far as the entire parliament is concerned, I only got the information that everyone else had. I can't remember whether any of that information was confidential, perhaps so, but not that I can remember today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just a general concept, sir. My question to you is this: If a member who was chief of police security, for example, in the security station in Prijedor, if he had a confidential memo, was restricted to disseminate that memo, would you, sir, expect to receive a copy of that memo?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a professional issue. He must send it to his superior in Banja Luka, and then the superior in his turn to the minister. And then should the parliament so require, the minister will inform a parliament committee. But he is bound to notify the presidency, the minister of foreign affairs was supposed to brief the president on the most important events on a regular basis. I think this also supplied to the municipal level, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was my question. Do you know if it applied to the municipal level? You're not sure, correct? You just don't know?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it did apply, but I'm not sure entirely. We should look it up to see what the law said about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, with respect to the mobilisation that occurred in September and November of 1991, I think your testimony in essence was that a very small symbolic number of Muslim Bosniaks, participated in the mobilisation call from the federal former Yugoslavia. Do you dispute, sir, the fact that the number of people who from Prijedor who actually were activated and were members of this mobilisation was in essence a fair distribution vis-a-vis the population in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I fully understand the question. What do you mean exactly by "just distribution, fair distribution"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My point is, sir, or tell us again, do you think that the mobilisation that occurred in September of 1991, whether or not both Muslim, Serb, and Croats were activated and indeed participated in the mobilisation or do you still think or believe that a very small few or symbolic number of Muslims participated in that mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about mobilisation for the war in Croatia. And on the basis of my own experience and what I had seen and in my contacts with people, my impression was that a small number of people of non-Serb ethnicity went to fight the war in Croatia, or responded to the mobilisation. The 5th Kozara Brigade was basically a Serb -- composed of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment, Your Honour, to find the text in which I can ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I told you, sir, that a witness testified here and felt or testified, and I'm referring to Dr. Donia's report, or the annex to his report, which is in evidence, on page 15, if he states: "The callup and deployment of the 5th Kozara Brigade was carried out without the support of the SDA, but many Muslims nevertheless responded to the callup." An OTP witness, Dr. Donia, would you disagree with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood that Your Honour had already ruled that this form of questioning was not an admissible form. It isn't admissible to put to a witness testifying what another witness may or may not have said, and then to ask whether he agrees or disagrees. He can put a proposition to him in ordinary cross-examination form, but not in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, would it be incorrect if I share with you that there were many Muslims who responded to the call, you would disagree with that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have already answered that question, on the basis of my own experience and what I have seen. And in the talks I've had with other people, the number was very small. As regards formal statistics, the members of the brigade and their numbers, I did not dispose with that information. But in the place where I used to live, only two people left from Kozarac, two or three people responded to the callup. From Hambarine, Rizvanovici, I think there were three people. From Ljubija, a few Croats, I believe. So I heard about a certain number, but it is a very small number compared to the thousands or ten thousands that lived in those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you know a gentleman by the name of Vahid Ceric?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would disagree with this: If Vahid Ceric confirmed to the SDS board that the percentage of each nationality in the TO unit corresponded to their percentage of the population in the municipality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I'm really tired now of hearing this question again and again, again. The witness has clearly answered and in the last answer added some facts. I'm not prepared to admit this question once more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you discussed the importance of a meeting that occurred in Banja Luka that occurred in September of 1992 where purportedly you saw Dr. Stakic. I'm just focussing your attention at that meeting. At that meeting, sir, do you agree with me that there were "very many soldiers" when you arrived. "The building was full of officers, soldiers, civilians, politicians, policemen, it was very noisy. There were arguments." True or false?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were people in uniforms and not wearing uniforms, and policemen and officers. There were many people. I don't know what the -- whether there were more of ones or the others. I was in my own specific situation, and I was concerned about myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Can you tell us, or estimate for us how many people were actually there in the September 1992 meeting, and what do you mean when you say "many"?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the hall above the staircase was full of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give me an estimate, sir. 1.000, 5.000, 10.000?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we're talking about one storey of a building. There could not have been 10.000, and now you're referring to 10.000. So, I think on the first floor, going up the stairs, there is a hall. It was practically full laterally towards the corridors. There was empty space in the other corridors. There are only people passing by, not very many. I cannot give you the exact figure, but there was a building and we know what building we're talking about. I can say there may have been about ten scores of people, and not hundreds. There may have been a hundred and some people, but at the moment, I simply did not remember the number, and I wasn't counting those people at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May of 1996, page 960 of your transcript, you describe for us the building was full of officers, soldiers, civilians, politicians, policemen. Can you tell me, sir, if all those people that were there, regardless of the number that you can't recall now, were they all just as important to the events that were taking place there, since you told us earlier about the fact that Dr. Stakic was purportedly there, it meant something to you. All the other civilian, politicians, policemen, soldiers, were they all important, officers?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, at the time Mr. Karadzic was coming to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Were all the people you've described --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my own experience, the people who went to that building at that time and on the basis of my own experience in the SDA and when the president of the state convenes a meeting, he doesn't just invite anyone. He invites politicians, officials, and not just anybody can come when the head of the state is there. On the basis of that, in that discussion, I said that I believed, and I still do believe, that someone who is not important in the structure of authority could not have been invited to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt before we have a break, may I quote from Exhibit D19A, the English version, page 21. I quote the late Muhamed Cehajic: "We can talk civilly without raising the atmosphere and voices." The trial stands adjourned until 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And I give the floor to the Defence for the last 90 minutes of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I'd like to acknowledge the Bench, and inform you I did take your comments to heart, and to the extent that something that was said in a voice that was inappropriate for the courtroom, I certainly apologise to the Bench and the witness for that. If I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, a couple more questions, if you don't mind. There has been some discussion regarding the official gazette and how it works. Is it true, sir, that, for example, if a constitutional court would make a decision, do you know if that decision would appear the same day in the official gazette, the day before in the official gazette, or usually the day after the decision is made in the official gazette?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, it appears following its adoption in the official gazette, but I don't know how long, what the time period is after the decision is made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you, if the usher would be kind enough to tender the first that document with the ERN number 00179941, I believe, or 9541. It's difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's apparently a 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it appears, it's one of our documents 65 ter number 372, in which case there must be a translation somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That very well may be true, Your Honour. I'm just asking general questions on this document, we're not going to have the witness read the document. If I may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, this is a decision from the constitutional court. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that it was adopted by the constitutional court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a decision dated when, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is October 8, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you expect, sir, to see this printed in the official gazette before October 8th, 1992, or after October 8th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know what sort of decision it is. I don't know what its substance is, and I cannot speak about the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, sir, in all fairness to you, has nothing to do with the substance of it, just the date. When would you, as a former member in 1991 and 1992, expect to see a decision by the constitutional court appear in the official gazette? Logically, one would think it would appear after October 8th, 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Logically speaking, the decision is adopted after a judicial proceedings. How long that lasts, I don't know. But in practice the constitutional court -- spends quite a lot of time in reviewing and adopting decisions. And some of these procedures are underway at the very moment now, and they last quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you the official gazette relating to this decision, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if I can have the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before you you have the official gazette of October 7th, 1992, or so it appears. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you see, sir, on the third page of the second document that I gave you, which I'm going to ask the Court to mark, that despite the fact that it's dated October 7th, 1992, in Sarajevo, there is a decision which apparently is being printed relating to October 8th, 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says October 8, 1992, and it is a copy of a decision which was published in the official gazette.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on top, on the date for this official gazette, what's the date on the top left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, it says October 7, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have both these exhibits marked as Defence Exhibit 20 and 21 respectfully, D20 and 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Hesitant, but nevertheless admitted into evidence, D20B and D21B. The latter is the official gazette. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have some, but can I just deal with my understanding of cross-examination and ask to go into private session over one aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Closed session, I think, actually rather than private. It's to do with the document that was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we then please go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I re-examine, there's one other matter I want to raise, the witness was asked a number of questions, in respect of the records of the Kozarac area territorial organisation that were disclosed. I want to understand, and I want the witness to understand, is the suggestion being made that this witness was involved in or responsible for in some way, or that there was, arming of the non-Serb population in order to launch an attack on Prijedor? Otherwise, I don't understand the purpose of the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you understand, it's an invitation to proceed with the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's an invitation to the Defence to make it clear what their case is on this, so that the witness can deal with it. Again, Your Honour, I keep going back to it, and it's perhaps not surprising given that we were responsible for it, but there is a rule that if a case is to be advanced at a later stage, either through evidence of the defendant or other witnesses, which in some way is going to contradict the witness, the evidence this witness has given, then it must be put to him. That's the only reason I'm raising it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I don't believe I understand fully what the OTP is suggesting. And I think, from what I heard, that they would like the burden of proof to be switched on the side of the Defence, and they would also, I believe, like to have the Defence put their case in its entirety before the conclusion of the Prosecution's case. It's not going to happen. The documents, as we have said in the past, as we've said with numerous witnesses, as the OTP herself has said, speak for themselves. The witness refused on numerous occasions to answer, what I considered respectfully, straightforward questions and gave us explanations that went on for several lines. We did so, with respect to the issues raised by the OTP. If the OTP feels they must rehabilitate a witness, they should do so on each and every witness. If they feel there was a suggestion made, then they should try to clarify that suggestion for the Court, if they feel it was a strong enough suggestion. The comments and the questions with respect to the Kozarac Territorial Defence were asked for a multitude of reasons, one of which was to test the veracity of this witness; secondly, to test the recollection of the witness. And third, comparing it to the testimony that he gave in several other trials that we have seen by my references to those cases. I'm not sure I can answer the OTP, nor do I think we are required to answer the OTP on these issues. We will be glad, when the time is right to establish the true context of the territory, how events transpired, and I think we have to some degree done that, so that the Court can have a complete and full and honest review of the facts. With respect to this particular witness, if we were to make an accusation, and if we were going to attack this witness, we would have certainly done so, Your Honour. We confided, and I think we acted appropriately in each of our questions to him. We did not ask this witness questions in areas that he was either not present at or was not being quoted as being present at certain meetings. We refuse to accept the invitation by the OTP and do not accept their attempt to try to shift the burden of proof and will not at this time be putting on our Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, again, Mr. Ostojic doesn't want to answer a simple question. But Your Honour, I've made the point. It's not shifting of the burden of proof; it is an obligation under the rules to put one's case to a witness. And I am taking it, from what Mr. Ostojic has said, that there is no suggestion and no evidence will be called at a later stage that Mr. Sejmenovic was in any way involved in arming of Muslims, supply of weapons, or anything like that. Because if that's the case, it should have been put. Your Honour, I'm satisfied with Mr. Ostojic's reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But it's of course free for the OTP to put such questions if they believe there could emanate a problem for the OTP from the questions and answers during cross-examination. I think that's the purpose of the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. But, Your Honour, I'm not going to put questions about matters which, contrary to Mr. Ostojic's assertion, and Your Honours will judge it for yourselves, Mr. Sejmenovic has dealt with and has repeated over and over again, that such arms, as the Muslim or non-Serb TO possessed were minuscule in comparison with the Serb artillery. Your Honour, that's why, otherwise I don't quite follow the point of the questions that were asked about it. But Your Honour, I didn't want to re-examine on that. There are two or three other matters I want to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think we should limit this to that of course we would be more than eager and more than happy to hear the final contributions of both parties on these issues already now, and not only the 20th of September. But we have to proceed as scheduled. And therefore, please feel free to put your questions in re-examination now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I want to ask you first of all, because it's the briefest, to have a look again at the record of the 14th of February assembly meeting in Prijedor. Could you have that back. It's D19. Now, it was put to you that Dr. Stakic at that meeting, in the response to Mr. Kos, was prepared to criticise other members of the SDS party. Could you just look, please, at the speech actually made by Mr. Kos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's at page 11 of the translation. I'm afraid, I can't help you in the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just have a look at what he said, after he said he greeted the assembly. Do you see this, Mr. Sejmenovic: "I wish to level criticism"?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that part. Do you want me to read this out loud?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'll just read it, and if you can follow. "I wish to level criticism against the SDS assemblyman's club and our people who participated in these negotiations. There was no assemblymen's club meeting afterwards, we were not informed about these conclusions, and neither were it seems many others. And that isn't all." And he goes on. Do you recall, I know it's a long time ago, Mr. Sejmenovic, there being an argument going on between the SDS members at this assembly meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any argument, but there were assemblymen who held different discussions in different directions. Some advocated the need to discuss the spring harvest, the refugees. Others said that we had to have extraordinary elections. And those were the differences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Yes. Thank you. You can put that away, now. Now, next, I want to ask you about the documents that you looked at today, and also earlier. I think you were first asked about them, if I can find my -- yeah, on the 24th of June, and that's -- I've forgotten what the number is, the D number. It's the documents that Mr. Ostojic took you through yesterday where your name appears.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: D7. I wonder if you can have those for a moment. Your Honour, can I just hand Your Honour this message. I'll show the Defence. It relates to Mr. Sejmenovic, his travel plans. The Defence can have a look at it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, although I want to re-examine, if Your Honours have questions that you feel you want to ask, I prefer that they get done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's limited, so please proceed that you don't feel limited in your rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I just want to deal with some of the things that were said during the course of these meetings. But first of all, I don't think you've actually ever said, who was making the notes of these meetings. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. And I can't remember. It may have been a number of people. Some people may have been taking notes just for themselves, possibly there was a recording clerk in charge of taking minutes. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting at all of this manuscript or these manuscript notes?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you just tell us, because I don't think you've ever explained or haven't been asked this, what exactly was this committee or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, I attended several meetings, and those meetings were also attended by the Territorial Defence, the police, civil protection, and chiefs of local communes. It was a consultative body reviewing the situation. Sometimes party representatives were there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it have any particular name, that's all I want to know. Something like the council for national defence or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Immediately before the war, which means seven or ten days before the war, it was called "Crisis Staff" formally. But I was no longer a member of that Crisis Staff, so I no longer attended the meetings. I mean, the Crisis Staff under the command of the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. All right. If we take the notes that you were taken through, was there any consensus of opinion, or was there a difference of opinion of how things should proceed, what should be done, particularly after the takeover of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a consensus, at least as far as I can remember, though several meetings. There was a consensus about several different issues, not to give -- not to provide any cause for an attack, to try and negotiate both in Prijedor and in Banja Luka and all possible ways. Also, for the TO to be placed at the disposal of general defence, if there should be an attack, which means to protect the population. That's what I can remember now. Any more specific discussions or talks, I can hardly recall, because I had over 300 meetings throughout those years, and it's very difficult indeed for me now to remember precisely any one of those meetings. There were people who did not have a realistic view of the situation, so they put forward proposals that were completely off the mark. There was a lack of consensus concerning the proposals by some people for a new municipality to be established. There was no consensus about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just have a look one more time at what you said, and that's in the meeting of the 6th of June. I think that's an error. I think it should be the 6th of May. Page 320 -- 319 in the translation. And it's you speaking, Mr. Sejmenovic. And it starts: "I can see two solutions..."

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find this. All right, I've just found it. "I see two options," that's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you just read out that part, because we've got "I see two solutions" and you say it's "options." Can you just read out so we can get a translation of what you said there.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This reads: "I see two options, without insignia or with insignia for the police." So these are the two options. "But the question is posed of the safety of the people, who will protect them after the disarming, if we turn in our weapons?" Two illegible words here. And then: "Many people will get hurt. If we decide to try to buy time, we must try everything possible. I am not in favour of leaving the people without protection. I would prefer for us to at least try to put up some defence, to try to successfully defend ourselves."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. First, have you any reason to believe that this is an inaccurate note of what you said?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure. I remember that it was in this context, and I remember that my view was, and that there was fear among the people that if we turned in our weapons, a massacre would immediately ensue, such as we have heard a lot about. I never suggested here that there was only one option. It was said that there were two options, and that we should choose either of those. But what was the most difficult problem for me at that time was how at least a minimum protection was to be secured. I, alongside with many other people, did not believe that it was logical to surrender under the -- on the terms requested by the Serbs, especially following the ultimatum where we were requested to hand over incredible amounts of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the two options that you were talking about was either surrender your weapons or hang on to your weapons to defend yourselves?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In order to defend ourselves, if we were to be attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was an option ever considered at any of these meetings that you, the non-Serb population, should launch an attack on the Serbs in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, not at any moment, not by any person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the final matter that I want to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't realise that Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The final matter that I want to ask you about Mr. Sejmenovic is this: It was suggested -- it was put to you in terms. You know that Dr. Stakic, as early as February of 1992, was a man who was not informed of what was going on in the municipality and did not even know what was going on republic, much less municipal level. And your answer was "no." From your knowledge of events and Dr. Stakic in the Prijedor Municipality, what was his role, his position in February 1992 onwards, or from February 1992 onwards?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that in February 1992, he was vice-president of the Municipal Assembly. I know that he was an official of the SDS. I think he was in the Executive Board. I'm not quite sure. He may have been vice-president, but I know that he was an official at any rate. I already said that I attended meetings when he was vice-president, and it was a well-known fact in Prijedor. From my own experience, I know that the post of vice-president or president is not attributed easily or to any person. It must be a person who in the political structure, in terms of hierarchy, was highly placed. This, I know, from my experience in relation to any party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible in your view for the vice-president of a municipality, subsequently the president of a breakaway assembly, to be a mere figurehead and not to be aware of what was happening or what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We object to the form of the question, Your Honour, both inappropriate as to what may be possible. If we're dealing with reasonableness is one thing. And secondly I think it calls for extreme speculation on behalf of this witness, in light of his evidence wherein he described for us not just recently, but in 2001 when he testified, as our questions were put to him in the Keraterm Sikirica trial where he did not know the post. That type of question is inappropriate we believe for both those bases, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question is on the level we heard during the last days from both sides, and therefore, I can't see a reason why we should change our attitude. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, Mr. Stakic, Dr. Stakic, was the vice-president of the municipality, president of the National Defence Council, later president of the Serb assembly. Now, from your knowledge, from your experience of political life, is it possible that Dr. Stakic was all of these things and was in ignorance of events and decisions in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to my mind, this is quite impossible. It is impossible to hold such a post, if you're not some sort of authority in your party, or to be so highly placed and not be informed of what is going on. Regardless of the party or structure in question, in practice, it is simply not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Mr. Sejmenovic, that's all I'm going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher, please, to present these documents first to the Defence, and then to the witness. For the record, these are the originals provided today for us by the OTP of the official gazette, Prijedor, issue number 2 and 3 of 1992. Mr. Sejmenovic, may I ask you, have you ever seen the official gazette of Prijedor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen the official gazette in 1992. Some on occasions in 1991, I did see the gazette, or perhaps in January, February 1992. But I cannot remember with precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was the official gazette always published in Latin and Cyrillic letters?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. This was according to the law. It was essential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore, the pagination between issue 2 and 3 is a different one. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How is it possible that issue number 2 of 1992 is from 25 June; issue number 3, 1992, from 31 August? Did you ever hear that there was a change in the board of editors or something like that who were responsible for the official gazette during the year 1992? Because I would be surprised that issue number 1 would have been from January, and then until June, no new official gazette. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can see here is not logical to me. As regards possible changes of the editors, in the official gazette, it is true that when the SDS took over power, all the non-Serb persons employed there were dismissed. And the officials and people at lower levels, too. So it is quite possible that there were changes there in the official gazette, too. But I cannot specify who was in question, which persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who had normally access to this official gazette in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, there was a service within the Municipal Assembly which was tasked with the following: That after sessions were held, they collected the decisions of the municipal parliament or government and other administrative decisions from the municipality, and to publish this occasionally in the official gazette. This was a service which was under the direct control of the municipality and who was the superior body to that, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And have you ever seen -- you mentioned maybe in 1991, an edition of the official gazette where the author appeared as a member or president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I haven't quite understood the question, whether I saw an official gazette dated in the year 1992? 1991, where an author appears? Whom do you mean when you say author?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are some decisions published. If you have a look, for example, in number 2 or 3 in the beginning, and what can you read under the decisions published there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, at the end of the decision, I see a signature whose president of the Municipal Assembly, Milomir Stakic, handwritten, and this is the typical form in which a decision is published in the official gazette, regardless of what decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You're looking now on number 2 or number 3?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm looking at 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you have a look on the other pages of this gazette, who is signing the there-published decisions?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, on the first pages, all the decisions were signed by Dr. Stakic. So the decisions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In which capacity, please, if you also have a look on --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In edition number 3, in the capacity of president of the Municipal Assembly. In number 3, I'll have to have a look. Also the president of the Municipal Assembly, Dr. Milomir Stakic. There is a whole series of decisions signed by the same person with the same signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Always --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So on page 4, there is a decision where -- which has been signed by the president of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Milomir Stakic. And then there is also a series of decisions also signed by Dr. Stakic in his capacity as president of the Crisis Staff. All the other decisions have been signed in the capacity of president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And now let me turn to my former question: If I understood you correctly in the beginning, you mentioned that earlier, maybe in 1991, you saw an edition of the official gazette. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever seen there a contribution or decision which was signed by also where you can read in printing that "this decision was taken by a member or president of the Crisis Staff"?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you in person, to conclude, have never seen these official gazettes?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, those gazettes I never seen. I saw some that were signed by the president, Muhamed Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, while testifying before this Court, you mentioned for several times the Serb Radical Party. Was this party active in the Prijedor municipality, and who were the leaders of this party in Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Prijedor Municipality, the Serb Radical Party, its supporters, appeared before the party was actually set up. Subsequently, in Prijedor, the Serb Radical Party was set up in Prijedor, and I know that either the president or vice-president was Mr. Vracar, I think his name was Stojan Vracar from Omarska or from a village nearby Omarska. I don't know who the officials were. But it never developed into a larger party, and it did not candidate itself for the municipal elections. They held events or party meetings in different places, but after the elections, they were not present in their parliament, and their activities were not felt in the political life of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: In your testimony of 29th of May and 11th of June this year, you said that in the meetings, Dr. Stakic spoke rarely. It's page 2, English version. "But on the occasions he did speak, it was evident that he held the same views as other persons like Srdjo Srdic. Their speeches were identical." Can you be more specific about the content of these views?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour. The SDS, its official positions were implemented through the municipal parliament. The speakers would come out, Mr. Miskovic on behalf of the SDS, or some of the deputies coming from the SDS, that the general drift went in that direction. I remember an SDS deputy, his name was Dragan Sidjak who was very moderate in his views. And sometimes his views differed from those of the SDS. Then there was another person. I don't remember his name. But the remaining portion of the SDS did not differ in their views. They would mainly repeat the arguments that had already been put forward by someone. And in that sense, Stakic was no different from the others. There were rare individuals who were different, and I mentioned the names of two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No further questions from the side of the Bench. Are there any additional questions emanating only from those questions put by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This, then, concludes the examination of this witness. And we have to thank you for being prepared to answer the questions of all participants here in the courtroom. Thank you for coming, and you are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The official gazettes may be presented again to the OTP. May I ask, what about tomorrow? We are still on schedule and have Witness Number 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Your Honour, we've got some more -- no, we've got the original of the document that Mr. Ostojic was referring to, the Senad document. I think Your Honours asked to see the original. In fact, the original's just another photocopy again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are based on a photocopy only. If it -- let's wait until the usher returns. But as regards witness 3, we have a list of potential exhibits. And what about proofing notes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are none, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are none. And the estimated length of the hearing?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour, we've said two sessions in chief, but I don't think it will take that long. We revised it. Although he has got quite a lot to deal with, I don't think it will take -- I would hope that I can finish him in one session tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good to know. And in addition, there was probably we can finalise this, still a dispute on two documents amongst the parties. Has this been settled until now? They were not admitted into evidence. Probably the registry may help me out, the two final documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You're probably referring to D13 and D14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We would ask that they be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. And may I ask, are there any objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, I certainly didn't have any discussions with Mr. Ostojic about these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it was in the framework of the witness before us, but I may be wrong. We heard this witness since June 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I honestly can't remember what the problem was, if any, but can I put it this way, it's one of the documents from the Tadic appeal. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think both are emanating from the Tadic appeal. The problem was the documents were disclosed under Rule 68 to the Defence, and then the documents were tendered by the Defence, but apparently there were some problems by the OTP on the admission into evidence. Therefore, it was still open. I had hoped that it was settled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm going to have to go back and have a look at it in the intervening period. Nor can I remember there was an objection from us if there was an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the meantime, please, the usher present the document from the OTP to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in addition, we've also found if Your Honours want it, the translation of the document that Mr. Ostojic asked Mr. Sejmenovic about, which is the Supreme Court decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We said it was one of our documents, and there was a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It would be helpful, because we have only the B versions of these two documents. And then I think there's no problem to admit these into evidence as D20, D21A respectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think we've got -- we haven't got the second document, the actual gazette. I don't know where that comes from. It's not one of our documents, but we have got a translation of the typed document. So I can now hand that to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you. Then this would be D20A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Then, can I just in the last minute, in the light of the present or the discussions that we had in closed session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just, I'm really eager to have a decision on these two documents -- sorry. If they may be, please, shown to the OTP. They were tendered by the Defence; and from our personal view, there is no obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My recollection was Your Honours weren't satisfied with these documents for some reason. But without, again, looking at the -- at what was said...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can expedite it, Your Honour, if I may, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Normally, I would say "quid tacet consentire videtur," to be silent, seems to consent. So if there are no objections --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can't say that, Your Honour, because I honestly can't recall anything about these documents at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You are not silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just be very clear with respect to these documents, Your Honour: If there is any indication from either the Court or the OTP or any representative that there is an inkling of fraud, the Defence does not want anything to do with those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understood this. And please remember, only it was our point that the document, I think, it was J3, should never be used in the courtroom again. And as regards these two documents, until now, we have no fundamental objections, and we are expecting them probably you can address it immediately tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, for the moment, subject -- you know, I know Your Honours admit a number of documents with a caveat. I don't object at the moment on the basis that there's a question mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you remember, in the beginning, we distributed the document on the admission of evidence, and it always can be reversed when we have fundamental objections --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's simple, then, to just give it an exhibit number and be done with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then please, for the registry, admit it into evidence under D13, D14. Then we have settled this. And then you had another point?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very quick one, Your Honour: It's merely, as it were, in the Old English expression, "firing a shot across the bows," in relation to tomorrow's witness, we've provided the same kind of document, this time to Your Honours as well as to the Defence. However, if the Defence are going to seek to ask questions about that, I would ask that there be discussion in the absence of the witness and a foundation laid for why those questions should be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this is the basis of our future procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This concludes today's hearing. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
